findings.who: A filer whose only 2025 energy cost was a home energy audit by a certified auditor. Nothing was installed.
findings.why_no: The question asks only whether anything was 'installed'. An audit is not installed. Only the help says 'energy audit counts', and the filer may never read it.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: credit of 30% of the sum of ... '3. The amount paid or incurred for home energy audits during 2025'; p. 3: '$150 for home energy audits'
findings.fix: Put the audit in the question itself: 'In 2025, did you (or your spouse) have anything installed at a home to save or make energy, or pay for a home energy audit?'

findings.who: A filer who put up a small wind turbine at a rural home in 2025.
findings.why_no: The question lists 'solar panels, a battery, insulation, windows, doors, or heating, cooling or hot-water equipment'. The filer reads this list as complete, and a turbine is not on it.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'credit of 30% of your costs of ... small wind energy property'
findings.fix: Add 'a wind turbine' to the list in the question, and say in the help that the list gives examples only.

findings.who: A filer who paid for air sealing in 2025, such as caulking, weatherstripping or duct and attic sealing, but added no insulation.
findings.why_no: 'Insulation' is the nearest listed item. The filer does not think of sealing gaps as insulation or as 'installing' anything.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'Any insulation material or system and air sealing material or system that is specifically and primarily designed to reduce heat loss or gain'
findings.fix: Change 'insulation' to 'insulation or air sealing (weatherstripping, caulking, duct sealing)'.

findings.who: A filer whose old gas furnace, water heater, central air conditioner or exterior door failed and was replaced in 2025 with a new unit that meets the efficiency standards.
findings.why_no: The question frames the items as things that 'save or make energy'. The filer sees the work as a repair or replacement, not an energy improvement, so the listed equipment does not seem to fit.
findings.line: f5695.furnace_if_any, f5695.water_heater_if_any, f5695.central_ac_if_any, f5695.heat_pump_if_any, f5695.doors_if_any, f5695.windows_if_any
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'Natural gas, propane, or oil furnaces and hot water boilers'; 'central air conditioners; and natural gas, propane, or oil water heaters'
findings.fix: Drop 'that saves or makes energy' from the question, or add to the help: 'Count any new or replacement unit, even one replacing broken equipment; we check whether it qualifies later.'

findings.who: A filer who installed solar panels, a solar water heater, a wind turbine or a battery at a vacation home or second home in 2025.
findings.why_no: 'Installed at home' reads as the filer's own main home, so the second home does not seem to count.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'The home doesn't have to be your main home.'; p. 3: 'installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025'
findings.fix: Say 'at any home you lived in or used in 2025, including a second or vacation home'.

findings.who: A filer whose battery, geothermal ground loop or solar array was placed in the yard, a detached garage or an outbuilding, not on the house itself.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'at home' as on or inside the house.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'installed on or in connection with your home'; battery 'installed in connection with your home'
findings.fix: Say 'on or for your home, including in the yard or on a garage or outbuilding'.

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 moved into a newly built home that came from the builder with solar panels or a battery already installed.
findings.why_no: The filer did not 'have anything installed'; they bought a house. The help mentions 'work on a new or rebuilt home you moved into', but a buyer does not think of themselves as having had work done.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1: 'costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins'; 'The residential clean energy credit (Part I) is available for both existing homes and homes being constructed.'
findings.fix: Add to the question: 'or did you move into a newly built home in 2025 that came with any of these?'

findings.who: A filer who bought insulation or other qualifying materials in 2025 and installed them personally.
findings.why_no: 'Did you have anything installed' suggests hiring someone to do it, so do-it-yourself work does not seem to count.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: for building envelope components, 'don't include amounts paid for the onsite preparation, assembly, or original installation' (the materials alone qualify)
findings.fix: Use 'did you install or have installed', and add to the help that do-it-yourself work counts.

findings.who: A filer who moved or sold a home during 2025 after energy work there was finished in 2025.
findings.why_no: The present-tense 'at home' reads as the home where the filer lives now.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1: 'A home is where you lived in 2025'; p. 2: 'more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025'
findings.fix: Say 'at any home you lived in during 2025, including one you have since left'.

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder whose condominium association or cooperative housing corporation paid a certified auditor in 2025 to inspect the building and write a report. The filer's share of that cost came through assessments or maintenance charges, not an invoice to them.
findings.why_no: "A home energy audit was paid for" reads as an audit the filer bought and paid for. The association hired the auditor, and the filer never saw a bill, so they answer no.
findings.line: f5695.line26a_if_audit (and with it the line 26b amount and the line 26c credit of up to $150)
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation"; p. 2: "3. The amount paid or incurred for home energy audits during 2025"
findings.fix: Ask: "In 2025, did you or your spouse pay for a home energy audit (also called an energy assessment or evaluation) of a home you lived in? Include an audit paid for by your condominium association or housing cooperative, even if your share came through dues or assessments."

findings.who: A homeowner who paid a utility-affiliated program or contractor in 2025 for a "home energy assessment" or "energy evaluation" (for example, a blower-door test and inspection) and got a written report from a certified auditor.
findings.why_no: Nothing they paid for was called an "audit". They read "home energy audit" as a specific product they never bought, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Home energy audits: "Home energy audit costs are costs for an inspection and written report for your main home located in the United States that: 1. Identifies the most significant and cost-effective energy efficiency improvements"
findings.fix: Describe the thing, not only its name: "an inspection of your home by an energy auditor or assessor, with a written report recommending energy improvements (often called a home energy audit, assessment, or evaluation)." Let line 26a then test whether the auditor was certified.

findings.who: A filer whose audit was performed in 2025 and billed in 2025, but whose payment cleared in early 2026, or who financed the audit fee.
findings.why_no: "Was paid for in 2025" reads as payment made in 2025. The instructions' general rule counts amounts "paid or incurred" during 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: "You may be able to take a credit equal to 30% of the sum of: ... 3. The amount paid or incurred for home energy audits during 2025"
findings.fix: Ask "paid for or performed in 2025", and let the line 26b amount question apply the paid-in-2025 rule from the line instructions.

findings.who: A homeowner whose contractor did a certified energy audit with a written report as part of a 2025 insulation or heat pump job, with the audit priced inside the overall contract.
findings.why_no: They paid for the installation, not separately for an audit, so they answer no to "a home energy audit was paid for".
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 7, Line 26b: "Enter the amounts you paid for home energy audits in 2025."
findings.fix: In the help, add: "Include an audit done by your installer, even if it was part of a larger contract, if you received a separate written audit report."

findings.who: A married filer filing a joint return whose spouse installed and paid for a qualifying biomass stove or biomass boiler, especially at the spouse's separate main home.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only whether a biomass stove or biomass boiler was installed and does not say you or your spouse; the filer reads it as asking about their own installation and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows, and complete separate Form 5695 for each main home, combining line 30.
findings.fix: Make the gate say Did you or your spouse install a biomass stove or biomass boiler, and treat either spouse's installation or cost as in scope on a joint return.

findings.who: A condominium owner or cooperative tenant-stockholder whose association installed a qualifying biomass boiler serving the building, with the owner's proportionate share treated as paid.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether a biomass stove or biomass boiler was installed as if by the filer; the owner did not install a stove or boiler in their unit and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.
findings.fix: Ask whether the filer or their condominium or cooperative association installed qualifying biomass property, and explain the deemed-paid proportionate share.

findings.who: A filer who installed a qualifying biomass stove or boiler for home heating and answers no to the parent question because it was not bought to save or make energy.
findings.why_no: The parent gate is worded as Anything was installed in 2025 at a home to save or make energy; a wood or pellet stove burns fuel for heat and does not obviously make energy, so the filer says no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Section B: Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home, including certain biomass stoves and biomass boilers.
findings.fix: Broaden the parent gate to energy efficiency improvements or residential energy property, or ask directly about biomass stoves and boilers without an intent-to-save-or-make-energy test.

findings.who: A filer who installed a qualifying pellet stove or wood stove but does not recognize it as a biomass stove.
findings.why_no: The gate uses the technical term biomass stove or biomass boiler; the filer knows they installed a pellet or wood stove but reads biomass as a different category and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 7, Lines 29a Through 29h: Line 29e. Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive biomass stove or biomass boiler that has a thermal efficiency rating of at least 75%.
findings.fix: Word the gate as wood, pellet, or other biomass stove or boiler, or provide examples of biomass stoves before the yes or no.

findings.who: A filer who installed solar panels in 2022 to 2024 and used tax software that showed Form 5695 under 'Forms and Schedules'. Their 2024 tax was too small to use the whole credit, so the 2024 Form 5695 line 16 shows a carryforward.
findings.why_no: Form 5695 attaches to Form 1040 and feeds Schedule 3, line 5a. The filer reads 'Form 1040 or 1040-SR and its schedules' as covering every attachment that flows into the 1040. Or they recall only the 1040 and Schedule 3 and answer no from memory. The gate asks about forms in general, not the credit, so nothing prompts them to recall the solar credit.
findings.irs_text: f5695 (2025) p. 1, line 12: 'Credit carryforward from 2024. Enter the amount, if any, from your 2024 Form 5695, line 16'
findings.fix: Ask about the fact, or add help text naming it: 'Did your (or, on a joint return, your spouse's) 2024 return include Form 5695, Residential Energy Credits, for example for solar, wind, geothermal, battery, or fuel cell property? Count forms attached to your return, such as Form 5695, even if they feed a schedule.' Or ask the line 12 question directly, defaulting to zero when it is blank.

findings.who: A filer whose original 2024 return was Form 1040 alone. In 2025 they filed Form 1040-X adding Form 5695 for 2024 solar property, which left a carryforward on the amended 2024 Form 5695, line 16.
findings.why_no: 'Your 2024 federal income tax return' reads as the return as originally filed, which had no other forms. Nothing says to count an amended return.
findings.irs_text: f5695 (2025) p. 1, line 12: 'Enter the amount, if any, from your 2024 Form 5695, line 16'; i5695 p. 1: 'Also use Form 5695 to take any residential clean energy credit carryforward from 2024'
findings.fix: Add 'as originally filed or as amended (Form 1040-X)' to the gate, or ask directly whether any 2024 Form 5695, original or amended, shows an amount on line 16.

findings.who: A couple married in 2025 who file jointly for 2025. In 2024 the spouse filed a separate single return with Form 5695 and a line 16 carryforward. The filer prepares the return alone and knows only their own 2024 Form 1040.
findings.why_no: The gate does say 'or, on a joint return, your spouse's'. But a filer answering about a return they never saw may answer about their own return only, and the help gives no prompt about a spouse's separate premarital return.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 13: 'A married couple filing jointly report their combined income and deduct their combined allowable expenses on one return'; f5695 line 12
findings.fix: Add help text: 'Include your spouse's 2024 return even if it was filed separately before you married; ask your spouse.'

locators: Form 5695 (2025), line 12; , Purpose of Form, "Also use Form 5695 to take any residential clean energy credit carryforward from 2024"; , Married Filing Jointly, "A married couple filing jointly report their combined income and deduct their combined allowable expenses on one return"

findings.who: A homeowner who in 2025 replaced a failed central air conditioner with a qualifying highest-CEE-tier unit for comfort or because the old unit broke, not to save or make energy.
findings.why_no: The parent helper asks whether 'Anything was installed ... to save or make energy'; they truthfully answer no because their reason was replacement/comfort, so the tool never asks the central-AC question.
findings.line: f5695.line22a_if_central_ac (and f5695.line22b_if_central_ac for any additional qualifying units)
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025 located in the United States'; p. 6: 'Line 22a. Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive central air conditioner'.
findings.fix: Drop the subjective 'to save or make energy' from the parent gate; ask whether qualifying energy property, including a central air conditioner, was installed in 2025, regardless of motive.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where the spouse paid for or installed a qualifying central air conditioner, including at the spouse's separate main home.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'A central air conditioner was installed' rather than 'you or your spouse'; the filer answers no thinking only their own home or payments count.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows. 1. Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home'; p. 3 lists '$600 for central air conditioners'.
findings.fix: Use 'you or your spouse' and, for joint returns with more than one main home, ask per home or otherwise capture the spouse's central-AC installation.

findings.who: A condominium owner or cooperative tenant-stockholder whose condominium association or cooperative housing corporation installed a qualifying central air conditioner and charged the cost through assessments.
findings.why_no: They answer no to 'A central air conditioner was installed' because they did not install it themselves; the association or corporation did.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'If you are a member of a condominium management association for a condominium you own or a tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation, you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation'.
findings.fix: Include association/cooperative installations in the gate/help and ask for the filer's proportionate share.

findings.who: A renter or other non-owner who paid for a qualifying central air conditioner installed in a home they used as a residence in 2025.
findings.why_no: They answer no because they do not own the home and believe the energy credit is only for owners.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025 located in the United States'.
findings.fix: State that Section B central-AC costs can qualify for a home the filer used as a residence even if not owned, or add an ownership condition if that is the intended rule.

findings.who: A filer who installed a qualifying central air conditioner at a second home used as a residence in 2025 and answers no because they read the credit as main-home-only.
findings.why_no: They see 'home' and the main-home language for qualified energy efficiency improvements and conclude only their main home counts.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025 located in the United States'; p. 6: 'Enter the full address of each home where you installed qualified energy property'.
findings.fix: Clarify that central AC is residential energy property and is not limited to the main home; ask per home used as a residence.

findings.who: A filer who installed a qualifying central air conditioner partly in a home used for business or rental and answers no because they think the business/rental use disqualifies the whole item.
findings.why_no: The gate and gated help do not mention allocation; they conclude no credit if any business use.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1: 'If less than 80% of the use of an item is for nonbusiness purposes, only that portion of the costs that is allocable to the nonbusiness use can be used to determine either credit'.
findings.fix: Tell filers to enter the nonbusiness portion and not answer no merely because the home has some business/rental use.

findings.who: A filer who shared the cost of a qualifying central air conditioner with a roommate or neighbor and answers no because it was not solely theirs.
findings.why_no: They think only the person who paid the whole bill can answer yes, so they say no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'If you and a neighbor shared the cost of qualifying property to benefit each of your main homes, both of you can take the energy efficient home improvement credit. You figure your credit on the part of the cost you paid'; p. 3: 'each occupant must complete their own Form 5695'.
findings.fix: Ask for the amount the filer paid; allow shared costs and joint occupancy.

findings.who: A filer whose central air conditioner installation began in 2024 but was completed in 2025, and who answers no to 'installed in 2025' because the work started earlier.
findings.why_no: They read 'installed in 2025' as requiring the installation to start in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1: 'For purposes of both credits, costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed'.
findings.fix: Ask whether the original installation was completed in 2025.

findings.who: A filer who replaced an existing central air conditioner with a qualifying new unit but reads 'installed' as only a first-time installation, not a replacement.
findings.why_no: They say no because they 'replaced' rather than 'installed' a central air conditioner.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025'; p. 6: 'Line 22a. Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive central air conditioner'.
findings.fix: Say 'installed or replaced' and clarify that a qualifying replacement central air conditioner counts.

findings.who: A filer whose qualifying central air conditioner was installed in a mobile home, houseboat, cooperative apartment, condominium, or manufactured home and who answers no because they do not think it is a 'home'.
findings.why_no: They read 'home' narrowly as a conventional house.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1: 'A home is where you lived in 2025 and can include a house, houseboat, mobile home, cooperative apartment, condominium, and a manufactured home that conforms to Federal Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards'.
findings.fix: Use 'home (including a houseboat, mobile home, cooperative apartment, condominium, or manufactured home)'.

findings.who: A married filer filing jointly whose spouse owned and lived in a separate main home and installed qualifying Energy Star exterior doors there in 2025, while the filer personally installed none.
findings.why_no: The helper asks only 'Exterior doors were installed,' not 'you or your spouse'; the filer answers for their own home/person, so the joint return drops the spouse's door costs.
findings.line: f5695.line19a_if_doors; also 19d_i, 19d_ii, and 19e if the spouse had multiple qualifying doors
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'If you are filing a joint return... Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home'; combine the amount on line 30.
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse install exterior doors...' and include either spouse's separate main-home doors.

findings.who: A filer who installed an Energy Star exterior door at their main home in 2025 but replaced it for security, appearance, or because it broke, not with the purpose of saving or making energy, and paid for no audit.
findings.why_no: The parent gate is worded 'Anything was installed ... to save or make energy'; the filer truthfully says no because their reason was not energy savings.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: 'Line 19a. Enter the amount you paid for the most expensive exterior door that meets the Energy Star program requirements.'
findings.fix: Ask first whether any listed qualifying item, including exterior doors, was installed; do not require the filer's subjective energy-saving purpose.

findings.who: A filer who reconstructed an existing main home; the exterior doors were physically installed in 2024 but the reconstructed home was first used in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'installed in 2025'; the filer knows the doors went in during 2024 and answers no, although the cost is treated as paid in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed, or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins.'
findings.fix: Gate on 'installed, or treated as paid, in 2025, including reconstruction first used in 2025.'

findings.who: A condominium owner or cooperative tenant-stockholder whose association or cooperative installed qualifying exterior doors and whose proportionate share is treated as paid by the member; the member did not hire the installer.
findings.why_no: They read 'Exterior doors were installed' and the line's 'you paid' as requiring personal installation or direct payment and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'If you are a member of a condominium management association for a condominium you own or a tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation, you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your condominium/cooperative association install exterior doors for which you are treated as paying a share?'

findings.who: A filer who installed exactly one qualifying Energy Star exterior door.
findings.why_no: The helper says 'Exterior doors were installed' in the plural; a literal filer with one door answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: 'Line 19a. Enter the amount you paid for the most expensive exterior door that meets the Energy Star program requirements.'
findings.fix: Ask 'Was an exterior door installed?' or expressly state that a single door counts.

findings.who: A filer who replaced an existing exterior door with a qualifying Energy Star door, rather than installing a door in new construction.
findings.why_no: They read 'installed' as new installation, not replacement, and answer no.

findings.who: A filer whose existing home was reconstructed, with a qualifying natural gas furnace or hot-water boiler installed during the reconstruction in an earlier year, and whose original use of the reconstructed home began in 2025; no home energy audit and no other 2025 installation.
findings.why_no: They read the parent helper's 'Anything was installed in 2025' and the child's 'was installed' as requiring physical installation work in 2025, so they answer no because the furnace/boiler went in during the earlier reconstruction year.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins' (costs are treated as paid then).
findings.fix: Gate on costs treated as paid in 2025, not only physical installation in 2025; include reconstruction costs when the original use of the reconstructed home begins in 2025.

findings.who: A condominium owner or cooperative tenant-stockholder whose association or cooperative installed a qualifying natural gas furnace or hot-water boiler and charged a special assessment or included the cost in maintenance.
findings.why_no: They read 'A ... furnace or hot water boiler was installed' as asking whether they personally installed it at their home, and answer no because the association/co-op installed it and they only paid a share.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to include installation by a condominium association or cooperative housing corporation and costs paid through assessments or maintenance; ask about the proportionate share.

findings.who: A filer who installed a qualifying high-efficiency natural gas furnace in 2025 as an emergency replacement after the old furnace failed, not to save or make energy, and who paid no home energy audit.
findings.why_no: They read the parent helper's 'to save or make energy' as a purpose test and answer no because they installed the furnace for heat and reliability, not to save energy.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6, Lines 24a Through 24d: 'Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive natural gas, propane, or oil furnace or hot water boilers that achieve the highest efficiency tier...' There is no purpose test.
findings.fix: Remove the motive language, or state that a qualifying replacement furnace/boiler counts regardless of why it was installed.

findings.who: Married taxpayers filing jointly where the spouse owned and lived in a separate main home and installed a qualifying natural gas furnace or hot-water boiler there; the filer personally did not install it.
findings.why_no: They read 'A ... was installed' and 'at a home' as referring to the filer's own home or own installation, so they answer no for the spouse's separate main home.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: 'If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows. 1. Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home.'
findings.fix: Say 'you or your spouse' and include each spouse's separate main home on a joint return.

findings.who: A filer who bought a newly built home and first lived in it in 2025. The builder installed a geothermal heat pump in late 2024, before closing.
findings.why_no: The parent question asks whether anything 'was installed in 2025'. The installation finished in 2024, and the filer installed nothing, so they truthfully answer no and the geothermal question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins"; p. 1, Caution: "The residential clean energy credit (Part I) is available for both existing homes and homes being constructed"
findings.fix: Broaden the parent gate: 'In 2025, did you or your spouse install anything at a home to save or make energy, pay for a home energy audit, or start living in a newly built or rebuilt home (including one that came with solar, geothermal, battery or similar equipment)?' Then ask for the geothermal cost of a new home when its original use began in 2025.

findings.who: A filer whose home was rebuilt after a fire, with a geothermal system put in during the rebuild, finishing in 2024. They moved back in during 2025.
findings.why_no: 'Installed in 2025' is false for them, so they answer no. Yet the costs count as paid when original use of the rebuilt home begins.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 1, Costs: "costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed, or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins"
findings.fix: Include in the parent gate: 'or began living in a home that was built or rebuilt with such equipment'.

findings.who: A condominium owner, or a tenant-stockholder in a housing cooperative. In 2025 the association or co-op installed a shared geothermal heat pump system for the building and charged members a special assessment.
findings.why_no: The filer did not install anything themselves and thinks of it as the building's project. They read 'Anything was installed... at a home' and 'Geothermal heat pump property was installed' as their own purchase, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation"
findings.fix: Add to the parent gate and its help: 'Include equipment your condominium association or housing cooperative installed for the building; you count your share of its cost.' Ask about the association share separately, then ask for the proportionate amount.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly who live in different homes for part of 2025. Only the spouse's home got a geothermal heat pump.
findings.why_no: The parent question names no person. A filer answering for themselves thinks of their own home, where nothing was installed, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2: "If you made energy saving improvements to more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025, enter the total of those costs"; p. 2, Joint occupancy: "These rules don't apply to married individuals filing a joint return"
findings.fix: Word both the parent and child gates as 'you or your spouse', at 'any home either of you lived in during 2025'.

findings.who: A filer whose old furnace and air conditioner failed in 2025. They replaced them with a ground-source (geothermal) heating and cooling system as an ordinary HVAC replacement.
findings.why_no: They saw it as replacing broken heating, not something installed 'to save or make energy', so they answer the parent question no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2: "Qualified geothermal heat pump property is any equipment that uses the ground or ground water as a thermal energy source to heat your home or as a thermal energy sink to cool your home"
findings.fix: Make the parent gate list the items regardless of purpose: 'In 2025, did you or your spouse install any of these at a home, for any reason: solar panels, solar water heater, wind turbine, geothermal or ground-source heat pump, home battery, fuel cell, heat pump, furnace, boiler, water heater, central air, insulation, windows, doors, electrical panel; or pay for a home energy audit?'

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 had only the ground loop or wells drilled for an existing system, or installed a system the contractor called a 'ground-source' or 'water-source' heat pump using well water.
findings.why_no: They read 'Geothermal heat pump property' as the heat pump unit itself, under that name. They did not replace the unit or do not recognize their system's name, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2: "Qualified geothermal heat pump property is any equipment that uses the ground or ground water as a thermal energy source"; p. 4, Tip: "Include ... any labor costs properly allocable to the onsite preparation, assembly, or original installation of the property and for piping or wiring to interconnect such property to the home"
findings.fix: Reword the child gate: 'Was any geothermal (ground-source or ground-water) heat pump equipment installed, including ground loops, wells or piping for one?'

findings.who: A filer whose heat pump was physically installed in 2024 as part of reconstructing their home, and whose original use of the reconstructed home began in 2025.
findings.why_no: They read the gate's 'installed in 2025' literally and answer no because the heat pump went in during 2024.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 7, Line 29a: 'Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive electric or natural gas heat pump'; p. 1, Costs: 'in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins'
findings.fix: Ask whether they paid or are treated as paying in 2025 for a heat pump installed, or first used as part of a reconstructed home, in 2025; do not limit the gate to physical installation in 2025.

findings.who: A condominium owner or cooperative tenant-stockholder whose association installed a qualifying electric heat pump and charged owners their proportionate share through assessments, where the owner did not contract for the installation.
findings.why_no: They read 'was installed' as asking whether they installed a heat pump themselves and answer no because the association did it.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation'; p. 7, Line 29a: 'Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive electric or natural gas heat pump'
findings.fix: Ask whether the filer paid, or is treated as paying, a proportionate share of a heat pump installed by a condominium or cooperative association.

findings.who: A married filer filing jointly who personally installed no heat pump, but whose spouse installed a qualifying electric heat pump at the spouse's separate main home.

findings.who: A filer who installed a qualifying high-efficiency electric heat pump in 2025 to replace a failed HVAC system for comfort, not with any purpose to save or make energy.

findings.fix: Remove the subjective 'to save or make energy' purpose from the parent, or ask broadly whether any qualifying heat pump was installed; eligibility turns on the efficiency tier, not the filer's motive.

findings.who: A filer who installed a ductless mini-split system that is an electric heat pump meeting the highest CEE tier, but who calls it a 'mini-split' and does not think of it as a heat pump.

findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 7, Line 29a: 'Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive electric or natural gas heat pump'
findings.fix: Explain that ductless mini-split systems and other electric heat pumps count; ask whether any electric or natural gas heat pump, including ductless/mini-split, was installed.

findings.who: A filer whose home was reconstructed and a qualifying electric or natural gas heat pump water heater was installed as part of that reconstruction in 2024, but the filer first used the reconstructed home in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the heater was installed in 2025. It was installed earlier, so the filer truthfully says no, even though the instructions treat reconstruction costs as paid when original use of the reconstructed home begins.

findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Section B: "Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025 located in the United States."

findings.why_no: The filer reads 'was installed' as requiring the filer to have installed it. The association installed it and the filer only pays assessments, so the filer says no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "If you are a member of a condominium management association for a condominium you own or a tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation, you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation."
findings.fix: State that installation by a condominium or cooperative association counts, and ask for the filer's proportionate share.

findings.fix: Use 'you or your spouse' and expressly include a spouse's separate main home when both spouses owned and lived apart in separate main homes.

findings.who: A renter who paid for and installed a qualifying heat pump water heater in the rented home they lived in during 2025.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks the home energy improvement credit is only for owners and reads 'at a home' as an owned home, so answers no.

findings.who: A homeowner whose home was reconstructed after damage; the insulation and air sealing were physically installed in 2024, but the reconstructed home was first used in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether insulation or air sealing 'were installed' in 2025 and the helper says 'Anything was installed in 2025'; the filer truthfully says no because the physical installation was in 2024.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed, or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins'.
findings.fix: Ask whether insulation/air sealing was installed or is treated as paid in 2025, including reconstruction costs treated as paid when original use of the reconstructed home begins.

findings.who: Married taxpayers filing jointly who owned and lived apart in separate main homes; the spouse installed insulation/air sealing at the spouse's separate main home, while the filer installed none at the filer's own home.
findings.why_no: The gate names no spouse and the filer reads it as asking about the filer's own installation; they answer no for their own home, dropping the spouse's separate-home insulation.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: 'If both you and your spouse owned and lived apart in separate main homes... Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home... enter the combined amount on line 30'.
findings.fix: Say 'you or your spouse installed, or paid for, insulation or air sealing at any main home, including separate main homes on a joint return'.

findings.who: A condominium owner or cooperative housing corporation tenant-stockholder whose association/co-op installed insulation or air sealing on the building or common areas and included the cost in assessments.
findings.why_no: They answer no because they did not personally install the material and received no contractor invoice; the gate does not mention association or cooperative costs.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'If you are a member of a condominium management association for a condominium you own or a tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation, you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Include costs paid through a condominium management association or cooperative housing corporation; ask whether the filer's share of association/co-op costs included insulation or air sealing.

findings.who: A filer who installed a vapor retarder or seal to limit infiltration, such as a crawlspace vapor barrier, but no conventional insulation or weatherstripping.
findings.why_no: They read 'insulation or air sealing material or systems' as not covering a vapor retarder and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 5, Lines 18a and 18b: 'Enter the amounts you paid for any insulation material or air sealing material or system (including any vapor retarder or seal to limit infiltration)'.
findings.fix: Name vapor retarders and seals to limit infiltration in the gate or its help so filers know they count as insulation/air sealing material.

findings.who: A filer who installed only weatherstripping, caulk, spray foam, or a door sweep to stop drafts.
findings.why_no: They do not think of those items as 'air sealing material or systems' or read 'systems' as requiring a complete system, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 5, Lines 18a and 18b: 'Enter the amounts you paid for any insulation material or air sealing material or system (including any vapor retarder or seal to limit infiltration)'.
findings.fix: Give examples in the gate/help: weatherstripping, caulk, spray foam, door sweeps, vapor retarder, and seals to limit infiltration.

findings.who: A filer who installed insulation or air sealing in an addition to or renovation of an existing home, but believes it is part of 'construction of a new home' and therefore not eligible.
findings.why_no: They self-screen at the gate and answer no, although line 17e permits expenses for an addition to or renovation of an existing home and line 18a should capture the insulation.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 5, Line 17e: 'You cannot claim the credit for expenses related to the construction of a new home. If you are claiming the credit only for expenses for qualified improvements to an existing home or for an addition to or renovation of an existing home, check the “No” box.'
findings.fix: Keep the gate factual ('was insulation/air sealing installed?') and let lines 17a through 17e determine eligibility; add help that additions/renovations of existing homes are not new-home construction.

findings.who: A filer who installed insulation with a subsidized energy loan or received a partial rebate or utility subsidy and paid the rest themselves.
findings.why_no: They read that subsidized energy financing/subsidies cannot be used and answer no to the gate, dropping the remaining eligible cost.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Subsidized energy financing: 'Any amounts provided for by subsidized energy financing can't be used to figure the energy efficient home improvement credit'; fs-2025-01 p. 11: 'A taxpayer may not claim a credit for the amount of the subsidy that is used to purchase or install qualifying property' and 'Rebates generally represent a reduction in the purchase price or cost of property, so the tax credit amount must be reduced by the amount of the rebate'.
findings.fix: Ask installed yes/no, then reduce the amount only by the subsidized/rebated portion; clarify that a partial subsidy or rebate leaves the remaining cost eligible.

findings.who: A filer who had insulation installed in 2025 but financed it with a normal loan and is still making payments.
findings.why_no: They answer no because they have not fully paid for the installation, reading the credit as requiring full out-of-pocket payment in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed'; fs-2025-01 p. 12: 'Financing costs such as interest are not eligible expenditures for purposes of the credit'.
findings.fix: Ask installed/paid-or-incurred; count the cost when installation is completed, excluding only loan interest, fees, and extended warranties, and do not require the loan to be paid off.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where only the spouse owned the home, ordered the work, or lived in it first. For example, the spouse had the attic insulated, then the filer moved in after the wedding later in 2025.
findings.why_no: The question says "with you as their first user". The filer reads "you" as themself alone and answers no because the spouse used the improvements first. On a joint return, original use by either spouse qualifies.
findings.line: f5695.sec_a_original (forced false; the 17c question is skipped and the Section A credit is refused)
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 5, Line 17b: "To qualify for the credit, you must be the original user of the qualified energy efficiency improvements"
findings.fix: Ask "Were they new when installed, with you or your spouse as their first user?"

findings.who: A homeowner who installed recycled-content cellulose insulation, open-box Energy Star windows, or an unused floor-model exterior door. No one had used any of these items in a home before.
findings.why_no: The word "new" reads like a condition on the product. The filer answers no because the material is recycled, or the item was a display or open-box unit, or it was not bought new in the box. The IRS test is original use, not whether the product was newly manufactured.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 5, Line 17b: "you must be the original user of the qualified energy efficiency improvements"
findings.fix: Drop "new" and track the IRS words: "Are you (or your spouse) the first person to use these improvements in a home? Recycled-content, open-box, or floor-model items that were never installed before count as yes."

findings.who: A condominium or cooperative owner whose association installed new windows or insulation. The owner bears a fractional share of the cost and checks line 32b. Another case is a co-owner who shares the home with a joint occupant under the line 32a rule.
findings.why_no: The association or the other occupant arranged the installation and uses the components too. The owner may not see themself as "their first user" and answer no. The IRS form provides for fractional shares and joint occupants.
findings.irs_text: f5695 (2025) p. 4, line 32b: "If you live in a condominium or cooperative and have a fractional share of the qualified energy efficiency improvements ... check here"
findings.fix: Add help text: "Answer yes if the improvements were never used before installation in your home, even if a condo or co-op association or a co-owner installed them and you pay a share of the cost."

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder whose association replaced the building's central boiler, central air conditioner or electrical panels in 2025. The owner paid a share through a special assessment or maintenance charges.
findings.why_no: The equipment sits in a common mechanical room and was installed by the association. The owner reads 'installed at a home ... that you lived in' as meaning their own unit, not the building, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: f5695 (2025) p. 4, line 32b: 'If you live in a condominium or cooperative and have a fractional share of the qualified energy efficiency improvements or residential energy property expenditures, check here'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'If you live in a condo or co-op, equipment the association installed for the building counts, for your share of the cost.' Alternatively, ask a separate question about association-installed equipment before this gate.

findings.who: A filer who bought a house in late 2025 and had a new furnace or heat pump installed before moving in. They first lived there in January 2026.
findings.why_no: 'Lived in during 2025' is literally false for this home. The form's line 21a says only 'a home ... that you use as a residence' (present tense, no year), and the statute does not limit the year of use.
findings.irs_text: f5695 (2025) p. 3, line 21a: 'installed on or in connection with a home located in the United States that you use as a residence'; i5695 p. 3: 'a home that you used during 2025'
findings.fix: Follow the form's wording: 'that you (or your spouse) use or used as a residence.' Add help covering equipment installed in 2025 at a home you moved into afterward, or state the instructions' 2025-use condition explicitly so the no is deliberate.

findings.who: A filer who installed a qualifying heat pump or water heater at a seasonal cabin they stay in a few weeks a year.
findings.why_no: 'Lived in' suggests a full-time residence. The help mentions a 'second home' but not occasional or seasonal stays, so the filer may decide a cabin they only visit was not lived in.
findings.irs_text: fs-2025-01 p. 5, Qualifying residence A1: 'used as a residence by the taxpayer ... such property may be installed in the taxpayer's second home'
findings.fix: Use 'lived in or used as a residence (even part-time)' and extend the help: 'A second home, vacation home, or a home you rent counts; a home you only rent out to others does not.'

findings.who: A filer whose new home was built with a 13 kWh battery installed in late 2024, and who moved in (first used the home) in March 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether anything 'was installed in 2025'. The battery was physically installed in 2024, so a truthful answer is no. For a newly built home, though, the cost is treated as paid in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate: 'In 2025, was anything installed at a home to save, make or store energy, or did you or your spouse first move into a newly built or rebuilt home that has such equipment (even if it was installed earlier)? Or was a home energy audit paid for?'

findings.who: A filer whose fire-damaged home was rebuilt, with a battery installed during the rebuild in 2024, who moved back in during 2025.
findings.why_no: Nothing 'was installed in 2025', so the filer answers no. For costs connected with reconstruction, however, the cost counts as paid when use of the rebuilt home begins.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins.'
findings.fix: Include reconstruction in the broadened gate, as in the fix above.

findings.who: A filer or spouse who added a standalone home battery in 2025 for backup power, with no solar panels.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about things installed 'to save or make energy'. A battery stores energy; it neither saves nor makes it, so a literal reader answers no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 4, Lines 5a and 5b: 'If the qualified battery storage technology has a capacity of 3 kilowatt hours or greater, then check the "Yes" box, enter the amounts you paid for qualified battery storage technology on line 5b.'
findings.fix: Say 'to save, make or store energy (for example insulation, solar panels, heat pumps, a home battery)'.

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder whose association installed a shared battery system for the building in 2025, paid for from assessments.
findings.why_no: The filer installed nothing personally, and nothing was put in their unit, so 'installed ... at a home' reads as no. The association's cost is not seen as their own.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'including anything your condominium association or housing cooperative installed for the building'. Then ask for the filer's proportionate share.

findings.who: A filer whose battery was installed in 2025 in a detached garage or outbuilding and wired to serve the house.
findings.why_no: 'At a home' can read as inside the house itself. The rule instead covers equipment installed 'in connection with' the home.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Qualified battery storage technology costs: 'battery storage technology that is installed in connection with your home located in the United States.'
findings.fix: Say 'at or for a home (including a garage, outbuilding or the grounds)'.

findings.who: A homeowner upgraded to a 200-amp panelboard in 2025 so a heat pump could run. The heat pump itself went in during 2024. The panel was the only thing installed in 2025.
findings.why_no: The outer gate asks whether anything was installed in 2025 'to save or make energy'. A panelboard does neither; it only carries power. The heat pump that does save energy went in during 2024. A truthful answer to the outer gate is no, so the panel question is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 6, Lines 25a Through 25e: 'If the enabling property and the enabled property were installed in consecutive tax years, then you can treat both as having been installed in the later of the tax year in which the enabling property or the enabled property was installed, regardless of which was installed first.'
findings.fix: Ask the outer gate as 'In 2025, did you or your spouse install anything at a home (including electrical panel, circuit or wiring upgrades), or pay for a home energy audit?' Or ask the panel question regardless of the outer gate, with a 2024/2025 window.

findings.who: A filer had the panelboard replaced in 2024 and installed a heat pump water heater in 2025, so the outer gate is yes.
findings.why_no: The outer gate says 'in 2025'. The filer reads the follow-up panel question in that same frame and answers no, because the panel work happened in 2024.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 6: 'For example, if the enabling property was installed in 2024 and the enabled property was installed in 2025, then you may choose to treat both as being installed in 2025.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'In 2024 or 2025, did you or your spouse have an electrical panel, subpanel, branch circuit or feeder installed, upgraded or replaced at a home?'

findings.who: An HVAC contractor installed a heat pump and also ran a new dedicated 240V circuit or added a subpanel. The invoice shows the job as one heat pump installation.
findings.why_no: 'Improved or replaced' reads as work on existing panels or circuits. A brand-new circuit or subpanel added as part of the heat pump job is not perceived as either. The filer may also not recognize the terms 'feeders' or 'branch circuits'.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 7, Line 25c: 'Enter the amounts you paid for improvements to or replacement of panelboards, subpanelboards, branch circuits, or feeders that were installed in a manner consistent with the National Electric Code, have a load capacity of at least 200 amps'
findings.fix: Add help text: 'Include any new or upgraded electrical panel, subpanel, or new wiring circuit added for a new appliance, even if it was part of the same contractor's job or invoice.'

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder whose association replaced the building's feeders or panelboards in 2025. The work was done so new central air conditioners or heat pumps could be installed.
findings.why_no: The filer did not install anything personally and reads 'at a home' and the panel question as meaning work they had done in their own unit. So they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Add to both gates: 'Include work your condominium association or housing cooperative had done to the building.'

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly, living apart in separate main homes. Only the spouse's home had a panel upgrade along with a new furnace.
findings.why_no: The filer answers about their own residence. The gates do not say 'you or your spouse' or 'any home'.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: 'If you are filing a joint return... Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home.'
findings.fix: Say 'at any home you or your spouse lived in during 2025'.

findings.who: A condominium unit owner who belongs to the management association, or a tenant-stockholder in a housing cooperative. In 2025 the association or cooperative installed qualifying windows, insulation, exterior doors, a building water heater or furnace, or a panelboard upgrade, and billed the cost through a special assessment or maintenance charges. The filer installed nothing personally.
findings.why_no: The Part II property questions behind the gate ask whether an improvement or property 'was installed'. A unit owner reads this as work they ordered for their own unit. They answer No to each kind of property because the association, not they, installed and paid for it. They do not see their assessment as their own 'cost'. The rule that treats them as having paid their share appears only in the 32b help, which they never reach.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation'; p. 7, Line 32b: 'Occupants of a condominium or cooperative who are claiming a fractional share of the qualified energy efficiency improvements or residential energy property costs must check the box on line 32b.'
findings.fix: Before the per-property questions, ask: 'Do you or your spouse own a condominium unit or hold shares in a housing cooperative that is your main home? If so, did the association or cooperative install any of these items in 2025, or charge you a share of their cost?' Make each per-property question say 'installed in your home or your building, by you, your spouse, or your condominium association or cooperative.' Ask for the filer's proportionate share as the amount.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly. The spouse alone arranged and paid for a qualifying improvement or a home energy audit in 2025 on the couple's main home, for example a condo unit titled only to the spouse.
findings.why_no: If the per-property questions ask whether 'you' installed or paid for each item, the filer answers No for items the spouse handled. Part II is then not completed, and line 32b is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2, Joint occupancy: 'These rules don't apply to married individuals filing a joint return'; p. 7, Line 32b: 'Occupants of a condominium or cooperative who are claiming a fractional share ... must check the box on line 32b.'
findings.fix: Word every per-property gate question as 'you or your spouse'.

findings.who: A filer who answers Yes for one kind of Part II property, such as windows, but leaves another kind unanswered, such as heat pumps.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed as false whenever not every kind of property has a Yes or No answer. One unanswered kind makes Part II 'not completed' even though a Yes was given. The 32b and reconstruction questions are then skipped, and the refusal for an unoccupied rebuilt home can be missed.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 1, Costs: 'in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins'; p. 1, Termination of credits: 'You can't claim energy efficient home improvement credits for expenditures or property placed in service after December 31, 2025.'
findings.fix: Require an answer for every kind of property before the interview continues. Alternatively, compute the gate as true when any kind is answered Yes, regardless of unanswered kinds.

findings.why_no: The parent helper names only 'Insulation, exterior doors or exterior windows or skylights'. A filer who did only air sealing can read that list as complete, answer no, and never reach lines 17a through 17c or 17e.

findings.who: A filer whose only Section B cost in 2025 is a home energy audit of a house newly built for them that year. They had no central air, water heater, furnace, heat pump, biomass or panel work of their own.
findings.why_no: They truthfully answer that no residential energy property or enabling property was installed, or answer No at 21a or 21b. The gate is then false, but Form 5695 still sends them to line 26 ('Skip lines 22 through 25 and line 29. Go to line 26'), so the audit credit is figured without the new-home question being asked.
findings.irs_text: fs-2025-01 p. 5, Qualifying residence A2: 'A taxpayer can claim the credit only for qualifying expenditures incurred for an existing home ... but not for a newly constructed home'; i5695 p. 1: 'The energy efficient home improvement credit (Part II) is only available for existing homes.'
findings.fix: Before line 26, ask a separate question: 'Was the audited home newly built (not an existing home, addition or renovation) when the audit was done?' Its Yes should lead to the same refusal. The existing installed-property gate can stay, because with that gate false, lines 22 through 25 and 29 are zero and nothing they cover is claimed.

findings.why_no: The parent gate asks whether anything was 'installed in 2025'. Installation finished in 2024, so a truthful answer is no, and the solar water heating question is never asked.

findings.fix: Broaden the parent gate: 'In 2025, was anything installed at a home to save or make energy, did you or your spouse first move into a newly built or rebuilt home that had such equipment, or was a home energy audit paid for?' Then ask the solar water child question in that case too.

findings.who: A filer whose home was rebuilt, for example after a fire, with a solar water heater put in during 2024. The filer began living in the rebuilt home in 2025.
findings.why_no: Installation was completed in 2024, so the filer truthfully answers no to 'installed in 2025'.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins.'
findings.fix: In the parent gate, treat equipment in a reconstructed home whose use began in 2025 as installed in 2025, or ask about it directly.

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder. The association or cooperative installed a shared solar water heating system for the building in 2025, and the filer paid a share through an assessment or maintenance fees.
findings.why_no: The filer installed nothing personally and thinks of the system as building or common property rather than 'at a home'. They may also not see their assessment as a cost of the equipment.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Add to the parent gate and its help: 'Include equipment your condo association or housing cooperative installed for the building, if you paid a share of the cost.' In the line 2 question, ask for the filer's proportionate share.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly whose spouse lived part of 2025 in a second home or a separate residence and had a solar water heater installed there. The filer answering the gate did not live there.
findings.why_no: The parent gate says 'at a home' without naming the spouse. The filer reads it as the home they themselves live in, unlike the gated question, which says 'you (or, on a joint return, your spouse)'.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'If you made energy saving improvements to more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025, enter the total of those costs'; 'These rules don't apply to married individuals filing a joint return'; Qualified solar water heating property costs: 'The home doesn't have to be your main home.'
findings.fix: Word the parent gate as 'at any home you or your spouse lived in during 2025, including a second or vacation home'.

findings.who: A filer who installed integrated solar thermal roofing, or a hybrid water heater whose energy comes at least half from the sun, and thinks of it as a new roof or a heat-pump water heater.
findings.why_no: The filer does not see the purchase as 'solar water heating property' and answers the child question no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Qualified solar water heating property costs: 'No costs relating to a solar panel or other property installed as a roof (or portion thereof) will fail to qualify solely because the property constitutes a structural component'; 'if at least half of the energy used by the solar water heating property for such purpose is derived from the sun.'
findings.fix: Add help to the child question: 'Include solar roofing that heats water and any water heater that gets at least half its energy from the sun, even if it also uses electricity or gas.'

findings.who: A homeowner whose home was reconstructed after a casualty and who installed a qualifying natural gas water heater during reconstruction in 2024, but whose original use of the reconstructed home began in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether anything was installed in 2025 and whether a water heater was installed; the filer truthfully says no because the physical installation occurred in 2024.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: 'costs are treated as being paid ... in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins.'
findings.fix: Ask whether the filer paid or incurred costs in 2025 under the Costs rule, including a reconstructed home first used in 2025, rather than only physical installation in 2025.

findings.who: A married filer filing jointly whose spouse owned and lived apart in a separate main home and installed a qualifying natural gas water heater there in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate does not say 'you or your spouse'; the filer reads it as asking only about their own home or installation and answers no for the spouse's separate main home.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Married taxpayers with more than one home: 'If you are filing a joint return, figure your energy efficient home improvement credit as follows. ... Complete lines 17a through 30 of a separate Form 5695 for each main home. ... enter the combined amount on line 30 of one of the forms.'
findings.fix: Say 'you or your spouse installed, or are treated as having paid for, a qualifying water heater at any home used as a residence,' including a spouse's separate main home on a joint return.

findings.who: A tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation or a condominium owner in an association whose co-op or association installed qualifying natural gas water heaters in 2025 and allocated the cost to the filer.
findings.why_no: They personally did not install a water heater; the association or corporation did the installation, so they read 'was installed' as no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.fix: Include installations made by a condominium management association or cooperative housing corporation and treated as paid by the filer.

findings.who: A filer who replaced a broken qualifying natural gas water heater in 2025 at home merely to restore hot water, with no other energy project and no audit.
findings.why_no: They answer no to the parent helper 'Anything was installed ... to save or make energy' because they did not install it for that purpose; the water-heater helper is then never asked.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6, Lines 23a Through 23d: 'Enter the QMID and amounts you paid for the two most expensive natural gas, propane, or oil water heaters ...'
findings.fix: Remove the subjective 'to save or make energy' purpose from the parent gate; ask whether any qualifying energy property was installed or costs paid or incurred in 2025, and list water heaters as included.

findings.who: A filer who installed a qualifying natural gas water heater in 2025 in a second home they used as a residence, not their main home.
findings.why_no: They read 'home' in the energy credit as limited to the main home and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Section B: 'Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025 located in the United States.'
findings.fix: State that the gate includes any home used as a residence in 2025, not only the main home.

findings.who: A filer had a new home built with a wind turbine that was finished and installed in 2024. They first moved in and began using the home in 2025.
findings.why_no: The parent gate asks whether anything was "installed in 2025." The turbine was installed in 2024, so a truthful answer is no. Yet the construction rule treats the cost as paid when the filer's original use of the home begins, which was 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins"
findings.fix: Broaden the parent gate: "In 2025, was anything installed at a home to save or make energy, did you or your spouse first move into a newly built or rebuilt home that included such equipment, or was a home energy audit paid for?" Then ask the wind question in the same terms.

findings.who: A filer's home was reconstructed after a fire. The turbine was installed in late 2024 as part of the rebuild, and the filer's original use of the rebuilt home began in 2025.
findings.why_no: The installation was completed in 2024, so "installed in 2025" is truthfully no. The reconstruction rule moves the payment date to when original use of the rebuilt home begins.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins"
findings.fix: Add to the gate: "or did you or your spouse begin living in a rebuilt home in 2025 that included energy equipment installed during the rebuild?"

findings.who: A condominium owner or co-op tenant-stockholder whose association or cooperative installed a wind turbine serving the building in 2025, paid from common funds.
findings.why_no: The filer did not install anything at their own unit. They read "installed ... at a home" and "a wind turbine" as their own purchase, so they answer no, even though they are treated as having paid their proportionate share of the cost.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation"
findings.fix: Add to the help for both the gate and the wind question: "Include equipment your condominium association or housing cooperative installed. You are treated as paying your share of its cost." Then ask for that share.

findings.who: A rural filer whose wind turbine stands on a separate nearby parcel or field they own, wired to supply their house, rather than on the house or its lot.
findings.why_no: The gate says "installed ... at a home." A turbine standing away from the house reads as not "at" the home, so the filer answers no. The credit instead covers property used "in connection with" the home.
findings.irs_text: i5695 pp. 2-3, Qualified small wind energy property costs: "property that uses a wind turbine to generate electricity for use in connection with your home"
findings.fix: Change "at a home" to "at or for a home (including equipment placed elsewhere that powers the home)."

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly who lived apart in 2025. The spouse installed a wind turbine at the spouse's own separate residence.
findings.why_no: If the filer reads "a home" in the gate as their own home, they answer no. The line 3 question itself includes the spouse, but it is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Joint occupancy: "These rules don't apply to married individuals filing a joint return"; p. 2, "If you made energy saving improvements to more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025, enter the total of those costs"
findings.fix: Word the parent gate and the wind gate as "at any home you or your spouse lived in during 2025."

findings.who: A filer who installed a residential wind turbine, or a combined solar and wind generator, and does not think of it as "small wind energy property."
findings.why_no: "Small wind energy property" is a legal label. A filer with a sizable or hybrid turbine may decide theirs is not "small" and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5695 pp. 2-3: "Qualified small wind energy property costs are costs for property that uses a wind turbine to generate electricity"
findings.fix: Ask about the checkable fact: "Was a wind turbine that makes electricity for the home installed (any size, including one combined with solar)?"
